background.definition: Thoracic aortic aneurysm (TAA) is a localized or diffuse dilatation of the thoracic aorta exceeding 50% of the normal diameter and involving all 3 layers of the vessel.

list.listitem: Incidence is 5.9 new cases per 100,000 persons per year.
Prevalence has increased in the last 3 decades due to an increase in the diagnosis from increasing use of imaging modalities.

Aneurysm of the ascending thoracic aorta mainly results from cystic medial degeneration, whereas atherosclerosis is most frequently associated with aortic arch and descending thoracic aneurysms.
Medial degeneration leads to weakening of the aortic wall, resulting in aortic dilatation and aneurysm formation.
Cystic medial degeneration occurs commonly with aging and is accelerated with hypertension.
Sporadic cases of TAA have a family history of this disorder independent of connective tissue disorders such as Marfan's syndrome.
Blood pressure control with β-blockers may reduce the rate of aortic dilatation. However, this is based on studies in patients with Marfan's syndrome. C
For patients with known bicuspid aortic valves, Marfan's syndrome, or other connective tissue disorders, order an initial TTE to assess the diameter of the aortic root or ascending aorta. B

Differential.Differential_Name: Myocardial infarction : ST T-wave changes on ECG and elevated enzymes; may occur with dissecting aneurysm
Acute pericarditis : Fever, chest pain worse with inspiration and lying flat, rub on auscultation, ECG showing diffuse ST elevation
Pulmonary embolism : Hypercoagulable state, pleuritic chest pain, hemoptysis, accentuated pulmonic component
Pneumothorax : Acute shortness of breath, pulsus paradoxus, hyperresonance on percussion
Esophageal rupture: Pain followed by severe vomiting or retching, SC emphysema

list.listitem: Most patients are asymptomatic at the time of diagnosis. Patients with expanding aneurysm may complain of midback pain or chest pain resulting from compression of intrathoracic structures or erosion into adjacent bone.

Large thoracic aneurysms may produce a mass effect by compressing structures like the esophagus, causing dysphagia; recurrent laryngeal nerve, causing hoarseness of voice (Ortner's syndrome); trachea or bronchus, causing cough, wheezing, stridor, hemoptysis, or recurrent pneumonitis; and vagus nerve, causing hemidiaphragmatic paralysis. Compression of the superior vena cava by ascending or arch aneurysm may cause superior vena cava syndrome. Patients with ascending aortic aneurysm may present with congestive heart failure resulting from severe aortic regurgitation (AR) due to annular distortion and dilation.

On examination, look for features suggestive of Marfan's syndrome. Diastolic murmur may be detected due to AR. Very rarely abnormal pulsations may be felt over the suprasternal notch resulting from a large aneurysm.

The best clinical predictors of acute thoracic artery dissection are pulse deficit to rule in the diagnosis and absence of sudden chest pain and a normal CXR to rule it out. However, clinical findings alone are not sufficiently accurate to rule in or rule out dissection.
See Clinical Decision Rules section for a validated clinical rule and its interpretation.

Thoracic aneurysms are usually diagnosed incidentally as widened mediastinum, enlargement of aortic knob, tracheal deviation, or a tortuous aorta on CXR. CXR and CT are the preferred initial tests in the patient with acute chest pain and suspected aortic dissection.

Contrast-enhanced CT scanning and MRA are the preferred tests to assess the anatomy and detect the size of thoracic aneurysm accurately. When an aneurysm involves the aortic root, MRA is preferable to CT scanning as CT images the root less well.
TTE is recommended for evaluation of the aortic root in patients with Marfan's syndrome or other connective tissue disorders and to assess suspected AR.
Considering the semi-invasive nature of transesophageal echocardiography, it is not preferred for routine evaluation of a stable thoracic aneurysm.
For patients with known bicuspid aortic valves, order an initial TTE to assess the diameters of the aortic root and ascending aorta.
Blood tests are generally not helpful. However, a normal d-dimer level lowers the probability of thoracic aortic dissection.

A clinical rule was developed in 250 patients and validated in a second group of 250 patients with acute back pain or chest pain and suspected aortic dissection. Three independent predictors of acute thoracic artery dissection were identified: (1) aortic pain characterized by sudden onset and/or a tearing or ripping sensation or both; (2) mediastinal widening, aortic widening, or both on imaging; and (3) pulse differentials, blood pressure differentials, or both. The likelihood of acute thoracic aortic dissection was 7% if none of the 3 predictors was present, 31% to 39% if 1 or 2 were present, and 83% to 93% if all 3 were present.

The ADD Risk Score identifies patients at high risk for dissection. Risk factors include high risk pain features (abrupt onset, severe, ripping or tearing); high risk exam features (pulse deficit, SBP differential, focal neurologic deficit, murmur consistent with AI, hypotension or shock); and high risk conditions (Marfan syndrome, family history, aortic valve disease,

Elective repair (open or increasingly endovascular) is recommended for ascending aneurysms of 55 mm or larger and descending aneurysms of 55 mm or larger in diameter. Repair at smaller diameters is recommended for inherited aneurysms. B

Blood pressure control with β-blockers is recommended for asymptomatic patients with thoracic aneurysm who are not yet surgical candidates to slow the aneurysm growth. Patients who do not tolerate β-blockers may benefit from calcium channel blockers.

Prophylactic β-blockade with propranolol was found in a small open-label randomized study of 70 patients to slow the rate of aortic dilatation and reduce the development of aortic complications in patients with Marfan's syndrome.

Recently oxidative stress and the renin-angiotensin system have been found to play roles in the pathogenesis of TAA; statin therapy and angiotensin II receptor blocker therapy may have a protective effect. A cohort study showed attenuated anurysm growth in a pediatric Marfan cohort. Randomized clinical trials are underway.

A meta-analysis of 7 studies with 1510 patients found a slowing of aortic aneurysm growth in Marfans patients treated with angiotensin receptor blockers in addition to beta blockers when compared to placebo.

Surgery (endovascular or open) is indicated for aneurysms that are symptomatic regardless of size. Surgery is also indicated for aneurysms with any evidence of dissection or rupture considering the high associated mortality.

Elective repair is recommended for asymptomatic patients with aneurysms anteroposterior diameter of 50 mm or greater and an annual growth rate of 10 mm or more. Elective repair is also recommended for ascending aortic aneurysms with a diameter of 55 mm or greater and descending aortic aneurysms with a diameter of 55 mm or greater.
Aortic root reconstruction is indicated in patients with aortic root dilatation or ascending thoracic aneurysm and AR of any severity when aortic root diameter reaches 50 mm.

Surgical repair of the aortic root or replacement of the ascending aorta is indicated in patients with bicuspid aortic valves if the diameter of the aortic root or ascending aorta is more than 50 mm or the rate of increase in diameter is 5 mm per year or more. Recent review of studies has questioned whether this threshold should be reduced to 40 mm.

A systematic review of single arm studies (no comparison group) of patients with descending thoracic or thoracoabdominal aortic aneurysm found a pooled operative mortality of 10.4%, and rates of 4.9% for post-operative stroke, 5.7% for permanent spinal cord injury, 3% for temporary spinal cord injury, 13% for renal failure, 3% for myocardial infarction, and 23% for respiratory failure. There was an association between use of the clamp and sew technique and better outcomes, as well as with use of a CSF drain.

Thoracic endovascular aneurysm repair (TEVAR) is a less invasive but effective option, but clinical trials are lacking. Despite the lack of trials it is becoming the preferred less invasive option, especially for older and more frail patients.

Observational data in 85 patients who had surgery within 14 days of symptom onset found that 32% had rupture and 72% had malperfusion at 1 year, largely lower extremity but also renal (36%) and visceral (20%).
Another observational study of 151 patients (106 TEVAR, 45 open) found similar mortality (HR 0.9, 95% CI 0.4 to 1.6). After 10 years 85% of TEVAR patients were free of reintervention.
Hybrid repair of the arch is a newer approach but has limited clinical data comparing outcomes to traditional surgical approaches.
A systematic review of observational studies found that intravascular ultrasound was similarly effective as angiography for deployment of TEVAR.
Aerobic exercise is safe provided the patient does not have a markedly hypertensive response to exercise.
For patients with an aortic aneurysm larger than 40 mm, order serial evaluations with CT scanning or MRA at 6 months or on a yearly basis based on the rate of growth. C
Mortality is substantially lower in operated compared with nonoperated patients. B
In one series, the mean rate of growth for a TAA is 10 mm per year. This observed rate of change may not reflect the growth rate in the overall population.

A series of 907 patients with descending thoracic and thoracoabdominal aortic aneurysm found an annual grown rate of 0.19 cm/year, which was higher with increasing aneuryms size. Almost all ruptures occurred when the aneurysm was >5 cm (93%) although 80% of dissections occurred below 5 cm. Once it was 6 cm or larger, there was a 19% annual rate of rupture, dissection or death.
For patients who do not receive surgery, rupture is the most common cause of death, with rates ranging from 42% to 74%. The 5-year survival rate was 39% in one series.

The most important determinant of rupture is the size of aneurysm. The 5-year risk of rupture was 0% for aneurysms smaller than 40 mm, 16% between 40 and 59 mm, and 31% for aneurysms larger than 60 mm.
In a large series of 14,229 patients, 30-day surgical mortality was 35% for thoracic aortic rupture, 22% for aortic dissection, and 7.6% for unruptured TAA.
Among operated patients, survival rates at 1, 5, 10, and 15 years were 92%, 77%, 57%, and 43%, respectively.
The incidence of reoperation after thoracic aortic operations was 5% at 5 years and less than 8.0% at 10 years.
For patients with aortic root dilatation and diameter greater than 40 mm, order serial evaluations of aortic root and ascending aorta by echocardiography, CT scanning, or MRI on a yearly basis. C

A prospective study of 2026 individuals with 4897 CT scans assessed the speed of progression, of whom 388 had a baseline aorta 40 to 44.9 mm, 188 from 45 to 49.9 mm, and 76 >= 50 mm. The vast majority (> 95%) were men. Growth rates were similar for smaller and larger aneurysms. In those from 45 to 49.9 mm, only 3.2% progressed to > 50 over 4.6 years.
Inform patients about the typical symptoms of aortic dissection.
Instruct patients to avoid competitive sports.
Instruct patients to avoid heavy lifting or straining.
Elderly patients with comorbidities and limited life expectancy have a high operative mortality risk and may not be good candidates for surgical repair of aneurysm.
Pregnancy should be avoided in patients with Marfan's syndrome and if the aortic root diameter is greater than 40 mm.
Enlargement greater than 45 mm is generally considered an indication for elective repair before conception.
Dissection and rupture are most likely to occur during the third trimester or at the time of delivery.
Prophylactic β-blockers should be used throughout the pregnancy; this recommendation is based on expert opinion only.
